title: Three-dimensional dopant distribution from a single, out-of-focus spectroscopic image
authors: Michael Deimetry, Timothy Petersen, Matthew Weyland, Scott Findlay
abstract: Increasing miniaturization of nanoscale devices makes determining the three-dimensional distribution of dopants increasingly important. In out-of-focus spectroscopic scanning transmission electron microscopy images, we show that dopant atoms appear as disks with radii relating to dopant depth, allowing the three-dimensional distribution of dopants to be determined from simple geometric analysis of a single out-of-focus image. Through numerical experiments on Si-doped graphene we validate statistical detection and Bayesian inference methods to quantify confidence and uncertainties while making the analysis more robust at lower dose. We present proof-of-concept experimental data from an Fe-doped spinel, retrieving dopant depth to within around 2 nanometres.
summary: This work presents a novel technique to map the 3D location of dopants in materials using only a single, out-of-focus spectroscopic image from STEM-EELS. By relating the measured disk size to the dopant depth via geometric principles and employing robust Bayesian inference, the authors achieve nanometer-scale depth resolution. This method is crucial for characterizing nanoscale devices where precise spatial mapping of impurities is essential.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of determining the three-dimensional (3D) distribution of dopant atoms within a material using only a single, out-of-focus spectroscopic image obtained via STEM-EELS.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrate that the dopant depth can be accurately retrieved (within a few nanometers) by analyzing the geometric relationship between the measured disk radius and the probe convergence angle, even in the presence of noise and host material scattering.
method: The methodology combines geometric analysis (relating disk radius to depth) with advanced statistical inference, primarily using Bayesian methods applied to the full 3D spectral data cube to quantify uncertainty.
model_or_system: The physical system is a doped semiconductor or oxide material analyzed using Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy coupled with Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (STEM-EELS). The core model relates the observed disk radius in an out-of-focus image to the dopant's depth via geometric approximations.
key_observables: Disk radius ($r$), deduced dopant depth ($d$), standardized score map ($z_{xy}$), and posterior probability distributions for model parameters.
important_parameters: Probe convergence semi-angle ($\alpha$), dopant depth ($d$), noise levels (Poisson statistics), and Signal-to-Background Ratio (SBR).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions include the geometric relationship $r \approx \alpha d$ and the assumption that background and edge shapes are constant across the analyzed region, though the Bayesian approach mitigates some of these.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the contrast formation mechanism (disk radius vs. depth), compare three analysis techniques (background subtraction, z-score map, Bayesian inference) across varying noise levels, and show validation by subtracting the model prediction from the raw data.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the core physical principle (depth-from-focus) using simulations, to developing and comparing multiple data analysis techniques (Frequentist vs. Bayesian), and finally validating the quantitative depth retrieval using complex experimental data sets.
why_interesting: While the core physics is materials science, the rigorous application of Bayesian inference and statistical modeling to extract physical parameters from inherently noisy, low-signal-to-noise spectroscopic data is highly relevant to computational physics and data analysis in quantum systems.
